extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated early-18th-century public interested in manners, morals, and letters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples drawn from a periodical (The Spectator) on social conduct, composing epitaphs, judging character by appearance (physiognomy), and how to treat reports and narrators. Useful for composing short moral/literary pieces and character sketches in a periodical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph style: diffused (luxuriant) vs close (contracted)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are written in a different manner; the first being in the diffused and luxuriant, the second in the close contracted Style. The first has much of the Simple and Pathetick; the second is something Light, but Nervous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two model epitaphs are provided as exemplars: the 'diffused' form expands on biography and pathos (long, narrative, pathetical lines about family and death); the 'contracted' form is terse and witty ('Here lies the Body of Daniel Saul, Spittle-fields Weaver, and that's all'). Use the diffused style for pathos and detail, the contracted for brevity and wit. Also offered: an epitaph by the deceased that withholds judgment ('Here lieth R. C. in expectatione diei supremi. Qualis erat dies iste indicabit.') — a stylistic device that turns praise into ironic suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy indicators for judging disposition and academic bent
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very close Correspondence between the outward and the inward Man; practicioners read eyes, nose, ears, brow, gait, dress, and gestures as signs of temperament, humour, and likely profession/learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit mappings given as examples: a gentleman's eyes reveal 'the posture of his brains'; the nose indicates 'the size of his intellects'; an overly visible/pert ear signals a man who 'fears neither God nor Man'. A contracted brow, downcast look, sober pace, hands dangling parallel to pockets signify 'Logick, Metaphysicks and Mathematicks in Perfection'. 'Belles Lettres' typified by a sauntering gait, one wing of the peruke backward, hand in fob, negligent swing, pinch of Barcelona tobacco, and a 'Noddle-Case' (powdered hair) — small affectations signal literary tastes. Grave stalking pace => Heroick Poetry and Politicks; unequal gait => Genius for Odes and modern Ballads; open breast and audacious display of shirt => tendency to the Military. These are prescriptive/diagnostic sign-readings for composing character portraits or judging students at an academy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-breeding: the performance of attention in company
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Breeding obliges a Man to maintain the Figure of the keenest Attention, the true Posture of which in a Coffee-house I take to consist in leaning over a Table, with the Edge of it pressing hard upon your Stomach; for the more Pain the Narration is received with, the more gracious is your bending over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigned bodily discomfort and a particular posture are recommended social signals to show interest and respect to a narrator in public spaces (coffee-houses). This is presented as a polite convention — the outward signs of attention matter more than inward engagement when social decorum is at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward narrators; 'Matter of Fact Man' unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: A Matter of Fact Man is one whose Life and Conversation is spent in the Report of what is not Matter of Fact; there are very few who can 'see or hear' (i.e., accurately report), due to incapacity or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of liars/narrators are identified: (1) those with impudence + strong memory (reciters) who repeat what they hear literally, and (2) embellishers who add marvel and impossibility through rhetorical skill. The essay recommends general skepticism: prefer not to believe sensational reports, and when disputing a fixed version, point to the many other plausible ways events could have happened (a wagering/contrarian tactic). Also notes that deliberate inattention is a practical social strategy to avoid being misled by partisan/party relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper conduct in grief and widowhood: capacity for sorrow as a moral quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain Equanimity in those who are good and just, which runs into their very Sorrow, and disappoints the Force of it... My Sorrow has converted all Roughness of Temper into Meekness, Good-nature, and Complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent urges that grieving appropriately is a mark of virtue and sensitiveness; rules could be formed to guide men from the acute transports of grief toward a sober, virtuous equanimity. Lack of sorrow where decency and truth call for it is criticised as a greater sign of blockheadedness than ignorance of literature. Practical advice: cultivate the capacity to be moved by loss; such sorrow refines character rather than weakens it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of a 'good end' at death (dying well)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chaplain tells every body that he made a very good End, and never speaks of him without Tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'very good End' is implied to mean dying with resignation, piety, and appropriate last acts (commending servants, making provisions, requesting private devotional moments). The funeral and charitable bequests (mourning garments for the parish, pensions for servants) are cited as outward signs of a well-ordered life and a 'good end' befitting a gentleman — useful as models when portraying or judging a character's concluding conduct.
